decisions.location: Preregistered additional analyses, p. 5 (chunk 15, chars 15690-16431); see also Primary replication report, pp. 2-3 (chunks 2-3)
decisions.quote:
In the results quoted above, Srinivasan and Carey (2010) reported p-values for 11 effects. We replicated all
seven that were p < .05. We observed p < .05 for the four effects that Srinivasan and Carey (2010) reported
as non-significant. However the size and direction of our effects were consistent with the trends reported in
the original paper. It is therefore likely that statistical power may account for at least some of the differences
observed between the original and replication studies.
Citation:
Srinivasan, M., & Carey, S. (2010). The long and the short of it: On the nature and origin of functional overlap
        between representations of space and time. Cognition, 116, 217-241 doi:
        10.1016/j.cognition.2010.05.005
decisions.reason: The replication tested Srinivasan & Carey's (2010) Experiment 3 claim that functional overlap between spatial length and temporal duration is greater in a congruent than an incongruent training group (N = 144 vs. original N = 34). In the primary analysis, the focal group x novelty interaction was statistically significant, F(1, 142) = 4.47, p = .036, partial eta^2 = .03, with familiar-novel discrimination stronger in the congruent group (dz = 1.17) than in the incongruent group (dz = 0.81), leading the authors to conclude that the SCORE H* claim was replicated. In the preregistered additional analyses covering all 11 effects from Section 4.2 of the original paper, all 7 originally significant effects replicated at p < .05. While 4 subgroup tests in the incongruent group (easy and difficult trial t-tests and Wilcoxon tests) reached p < .05 where the smaller original sample had reported non-significance or a marginal trend (p = .06), the authors explicitly synthesize these 4 tests as consistent in size and direction with the original trends and attribute their statistical significance to higher statistical power in the replication rather than a contradiction of the original findings.
